sentences.text: Gargantuavis is an extinct genus of large, primitive birds that contains only one species, Gargantuavis philoinos.

The shape of Gargantuavis's head is unknown because no cranial remains have been discovered, and the single known cervical vertebra suggests it had a long, slender neck that likely precluded a massive skull.
Knowledge of this animal comes from limited skeletal parts including the synsacrum, ilia, and at least one partial femur that fits the pelvis.
Besides its large size, the pelvis was the most unusual feature of Gargantuavis.
Gargantuavis is the largest known bird from the Mesozoic era, weighing approximately 141 kg and standing between the size of a cassowary and an ostrich.
Histology shows Gargantuavis grew rapidly before slowing down for at least 10 years before reaching sexual maturity, a pattern seen in extinct moas and kiwis.
The first fossil of Gargantuavis was discovered in 1995 in the Var department of southeastern France.
The first fossils of Gargantuavis were found in the Marnes Rouges Inferieures formation, dated to approximately 71 million years ago.
The genus Gargantuavis was named by Buffetaut and Le Loeuff in 1998.
Analysis of its femur indicates Gargantuavis was a graviportal animal adapted for supporting weight rather than for running.
The broad structure of Gargantuavis's pelvis indicates it was not capable of fast running.
Because no cranial material of Gargantuavis is known, its diet remains undetermined.
Sediment analysis indicates Gargantuavis lived in a semi-arid environment with high seasonal climate variation.
It is hypothesized that Gargantuavis may have lived in environments far from rivers and floodplains, which would explain the rarity of its fossils.
Gargantuavis is the sole member of the monotypic family Gargantuaviidae.

Gargantuavis was initially thought to be related to Patagopteryx, but later studies placed it in the monotypic family Gargantuaviidae within Ornithurae, making it more closely related to modern birds.
Analysis of the femur identified Gargantuavis as a member of Ornithuromorpha, a lineage related to modern birds, and the sole member of the family Gargantuaviidae.
The shape of its femur suggests Gargantuavis was not a giant member of the Enantiornithes, an archaic group of birds.
Fossils of Gargantuavis date to 73.5 and 71.5 million years ago and have been found in northern Spain, southern France, and Romania.
During the Late Cretaceous, the regions where Gargantuavis fossils are found were part of the Ibero-Armorican island in the Tethys Sea.
Gargantuavis likely inhabited environments unfavorable for fossilization, such as rivers and alluvial plains, which make up most fossil sites on the island.
Gargantuavis lived from the late Campanian to the early Maastrichtian stages of the Late Cretaceous.
Research suggests Gargantuavis possesses primitive features, challenging earlier views that it was closely related to modern birds.
The ecological role of Gargantuavis is debated because it coexisted with large predators like abelisaurid and dromaeosaurid theropods, unlike giant Cenozoic birds.
Unlike many Cenozoic giant land birds that evolved without large predators, Gargantuavis coexisted with abelisaurids and dromaeosaurids, creating mystery about its habits and role.
Some researchers suggested Gargantuavis was a giant pterosaur rather than a bird, but this hypothesis was rejected due to bird-like features.
In 2009, researchers proposed Gargantuavis might have been a giant pterosaur, but studying bone shape and internal structure confirmed its identity as an avialan.
Other authors questioned the classification of Gargantuavis, claiming it was a basal ornithurine similar to Hesperornithies, while the original study authors maintained their cautious conclusion.
It is debated whether Gargantuavis belongs to Ornithothoraces, the group including modern birds and their closest ancestors, due to fragmentary fossil evidence.
